longForm.title: Operation Entebbe, 1976: Fifty-Three Minutes at the End of the World
longForm.excerpt: On the night of July 3-4, 1976, Israeli commandos flew 4,000 kilometres to Uganda, assaulted a hijacked terminal, killed seven hijackers, and flew home. One commando died. The operation's full intelligence record has still not been released.
paragraphs: The Israeli government's official account of Operation Entebbe — released in stages between 1976 and subsequent decades as operational details were cleared for publication — begins, as official accounts generally do, at a remove from the operational reality. What the declassified record shows, assembled across multiple countries' archives and survivor accounts, is a raid that succeeded because of intelligence that has still not been fully disclosed, a deception that came within seconds of failing, and a decision made by Ugandan soldiers in the final moments of the withdrawal that determined whether the mission left Uganda with one dead commando or fifty.

Air France Flight 139 was hijacked on June 27, 1976, shortly after departing Athens for Paris with 248 passengers and 12 crew. The hijackers were Wilfried Böse and Brigitte Kuhlmann, members of the West German Revolutionäre Zellen, and at least two members of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine — External Operations. The operation's organizational sponsorship has been contested in historical accounts, but the PFLP-EO connection is documented. The precise role of Wadi Haddad, who led the PFLP-EO's external operations until his death in 1978, has been established through East German Stasi records opened after reunification. Documents from the BStU — the German authority that administered Stasi records — include correspondence between Haddad and Stasi officers that postdates the Entebbe hijacking. The operational relationship between the Stasi and Palestinian militant groups in this period is one of the better-documented aspects of Cold War proxy conflict.

The aircraft was diverted first to Benghazi for refueling, then to Entebbe, Uganda. By July 1, approximately 148 non-Israeli passengers had been released. What remained was 94 Israeli and Jewish passengers, the 12 Air France crew members who refused to depart with the released hostages, and 7 hijackers. The holding location was the old terminal building at Entebbe International Airport, where Idi Amin's government had provided support, supplies, and Ugandan soldiers as additional guards. Amin visited the hostages in person at least twice. The structure and layout of the old terminal are relevant to what followed: the building's precise dimensions, door placements, and interior configuration appear in the Israeli operational planning record.

The Israeli cabinet's decision to attempt a rescue is documented in records of the deliberations themselves. Defense Minister Shimon Peres backed the military option; Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, by his own later account, was not persuaded until the military presented a plan he considered credible rather than suicidal. The plan's credibility rested on Mossad intelligence. Some of this intelligence came from Israelis who had helped construct or advise on Ugandan military infrastructure during an earlier period of Israeli-Ugandan cooperation — a relationship Amin had severed when he expelled Israeli advisers in 1972. The architecture of the terminal, at least, had not changed. The full scope of what the Mossad knew about the interior layout and the Ugandan guard rotation has not been publicly disclosed.

The assault force — drawn from the General Staff Reconnaissance Unit (Sayeret Matkal), the 35th Parachute Brigade, and supporting units — flew in four C-130 Hercules from Sharm el-Sheikh on the evening of July 3. The route covered approximately 4,000 kilometres, following a low-level path over the Red Sea to reduce radar exposure. A medical relay aircraft flew toward Nairobi simultaneously. The element of surprise at the terminal depended on a deception: a black Mercedes limousine of the model used by Idi Amin's motorcade, followed by two Land Rovers, drove from the lead aircraft toward the terminal in darkness. The Ugandan sentries at the terminal gate, seeing a motorcade approaching, initially did not fire. Then, as the vehicles came closer, they did.

The Mercedes stopped. The assault teams broke from the vehicles and moved on the terminal. Lt. Col. Yonatan Netanyahu, commanding the ground assault element, was struck by a bullet during the final withdrawal to the aircraft — exactly when and from where has been disputed between the accounts of soldiers who were present in the withdrawal sequence. He was the only Israeli commando killed. The operational timeline, as recorded in subsequent Israeli accounts: the lead assault team entered the old terminal at approximately 11:01 p.m. local time. By 11:54, the last of the surviving hostages were being loaded onto the aircraft. The 53 minutes between those timestamps encompassed the killing of all seven hijackers, the evacuation of the surviving hostages, the destruction of eleven Ugandan MiG-17 and MiG-21 aircraft on the runway to prevent pursuit, and the death of Netanyahu.

Three hostages died during the assault. A fourth, Dora Bloch — a 74-year-old dual British-Israeli citizen who had been taken to Mulago Hospital in Kampala on July 3 after choking on food — was murdered by Ugandan security forces after the raid. The British Foreign Office record of its attempts to obtain information about her from Amin's government exists in the National Archives. It is not a long record. Amin's government denied knowledge of her fate. Her remains were found in 2014, buried in a field outside Kampala. The Ugandan soldiers responsible have never faced legal proceedings.

The Kenyan government under President Jomo Kenyatta provided the Israeli aircraft with refueling rights at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where the rescued hostages were transferred and the wounded received initial treatment before flying to Israel. Kenya's role was not officially acknowledged for years; Kenyatta had reasons for discretion. The intelligence and operational coordination between Israel and Kenya in the period around the raid has been partially documented through the accounts of participants. Former Mossad officer Rafi Eitan, who has spoken publicly about his role in the coordination, confirmed that Kenyan cooperation was arranged before the aircraft departed Israel. The full diplomatic record has not been released by either government.

What Entebbe established, at the level of doctrine and its dissemination, was that counterterrorist hostage rescue at extreme range was operationally feasible given sufficient intelligence and preparation time. The German GSG-9's rescue of Lufthansa Flight 181 at Mogadishu in October 1977 was explicitly studied against the Entebbe template; GSG-9's commander Ulrich Wegener had observed Israeli training in the period between the two raids. The United States' own hostage rescue capability — formalized as 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment-Delta in 1977 under Colonel Charles Beckwith — drew on the same template. Beckwith attended planning discussions at some level; the records of those discussions have not been made public. The capability they helped produce failed at Desert One in April 1980. The template itself has survived.

shortForm.title: Venona: The Code That Named the Spies
shortForm.excerpt: From 1943 to 1980, US cryptanalysts decrypted thousands of Soviet intelligence cables using a mistake the KGB made once under wartime pressure and could never unmake. The program was declassified in 1995. Some of it still isn't.
paragraphs: The Venona program's public record begins not with the 1995 declassification but with a workstation opened at Arlington Hall, Virginia, on February 1, 1943, by a 23-year-old civilian cryptanalyst named Gene Grabeel. The program she initiated — a systematic effort to decrypt Soviet diplomatic and intelligence cable traffic — ran until 1980. Its existence was kept from the State Department, from most of Congress, and from President Truman himself for years after it began producing results. The NSA's own historical account of Venona, 'The Venona Story,' released publicly in the late 1990s, confirms that the operational secrecy was maintained partly out of concern that disclosure would reveal the source of the break — which was a Soviet error the Soviets had not yet realized they had made.

The Soviet cryptographic error that made Venona possible was the reuse of one-time pad key material. A one-time pad, used correctly, is theoretically unbreakable: each key is used once and destroyed. Between 1942 and 1943, under wartime material pressure, the KGB's cipher center in Moscow produced and distributed approximately 35,000 pages of duplicate one-time pad keys. Cryptanalysts at Arlington Hall, led by Meredith Gardner, identified the duplication in 1943 and began exploiting it. The process of breaking individual messages took years, and many were only partially decrypted — meaning that a given message might yield intelligible fragments while leaving other portions unresolved. The program produced partial translations of approximately 3,000 out of an estimated 200,000 Soviet messages from the wartime period. What was in those 3,000 messages was sufficient to identify hundreds of Soviet agents operating in the United States, Britain, Canada, and Australia.

The identifications Venona produced include names that entered the historical record through other means — Julius Rosenberg, David Greenglass, Harry Gold, Klaus Fuchs — and names that remained contested for decades afterward. Alger Hiss's guilt, disputed from his 1950 conviction through the 1990s, was corroborated by VENONA cable 1822, dated March 30, 1945, which referenced an agent with characteristics matching Hiss under the cover name ALES. The cable's interpretation was disputed by Hiss's supporters until corroborating material from KGB archives, accessed by Russian-American historians John Earl Haynes and Harvey Klehr in the post-Soviet period, established the identification on independent grounds. Donald Maclean — one of the Cambridge Five, identified in Venona as agent HOMER — was warned through Kim Philby in 1951 and defected to the Soviet Union before he could be arrested. Philby's access to Venona intelligence, which he had acquired through his liaison role with US intelligence in Washington, is documented; the precise chain by which the warning reached Maclean before his arrest has been reconstructed but not fully resolved.

The program was not disclosed to the public until October 1995, when the NSA and CIA released approximately 2,900 Venona cables simultaneously. The decision to maintain classification for fifteen years after the program ended in 1980 has been defended by former intelligence officers as protection of sources and methods, and criticized by historians who note that the secrecy prevented the full public record of Soviet espionage from being established during the period when it was most politically contested. The KGB archive material accessed by Haynes and Klehr in the 1990s, combined with the Venona release, produced the documentary foundation for the current scholarly consensus on wartime Soviet espionage in the United States. Whether the estimated 197,000 Soviet messages never decrypted would add materially to that record is a question that cannot currently be answered. Those materials remain classified.

sources.label: John Earl Haynes and Harvey Klehr, 'Venona: Decoding Soviet Espionage in America' (1999) — Yale University Press

onThisDay.headline: German Forces in Northwest Europe Surrender at Lüneburg Heath
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1945, Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery accepted the unconditional surrender of all German forces in the Netherlands, northwest Germany, and Denmark at his tactical headquarters on Lüneburg Heath, south of Hamburg. The instrument of surrender was signed at 6:20 p.m. local time and came into effect at 8:00 a.m. the following morning, covering an estimated one million German troops. The formal surrender of all German armed forces followed on May 7–8.
